title: Sickle Automation
protocolOverview: This protocol lets approved automators act on Sickle positions on behalf of their owners. `Automation` exposes two dispatch routes: fixed typed entrypoints for harvest, compound, exit, rebalance and dust deposit, and a generic `executeFor` where an admin binds a (strategy, selector) pair to a permission bit. Every action requires both the automator's permission and the Sickle owner's consent, plus a per-position opt-in stored in `NftSettingsRegistry` or in a pluggable `ISettingsModule` such as `MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry`. `NftFarmStrategy` drives the NFT position lifecycle with target geometry derived by `ShiftMath`, `MultiFarmStrategy` consolidates rewards from many positions into one destination, and `GasAccount` with the per-chain `GasCostAdapter` reimburses keepers from a prepaid native-token balance.
auditScope: This audit covers 16 smart contracts totaling approximately 2050 lines of code across 8 days of review.
overallAssessment: No critical or high severity issues were identified. The recurring theme instead is that the position an entrypoint validates is often not the asset the operation acts on: opt-ins bind an action's source more tightly than its destination or its removal source, safeguards are attached to a specific entrypoint rather than to the operation itself, and user-registered callbacks run inside shared keeper batches. A smaller cluster concerns gas accounting, which reimburses per operation costs that the chain charges per transaction.

evaluations.description: Authorization is layered and fail-closed, requiring the automator's permission, the owner's consent and a per-position opt-in. The weakness is enforcement rather than model, and it is systematic: most findings validate one position while acting on parameters never bound to it.
Little arithmetic overall, but the rebalance tick geometry holds the only mathematical issue. The remainder is gas accounting, allocating per-transaction costs per batch item.

Each piece reads well alone, but the system carries two dispatch routes to the same strategy functions, optional callbacks, pluggable settings modules and per-chain fee adapters. EIP-170 pressure also splits the rebalance checks across a call boundary.
Solid base: Solmate, OpenZeppelin clones and an internal library pattern that keeps strategies under the bytecode limit.

Configuration sits behind plain admin roles: the automator allowlist, the action registry, and the caller and target allowlists, with the timelock covering only settings modules. Nearly every finding requires an authorized automator, so the practical security boundary is the keeper.

In-code documentation is unusually thorough and often explains rationale rather than restating the code. The weakness is accuracy drift: some comments assert security properties the implementation does not provide.

The suite is extensive and fork-based, with per-integration harnesses across many chains. The gaps fall in one place: cases are overwhelmingly single-entity, whereas most findings need a second position, a second NFT, or the other dispatch route to surface.

issues.title: Automated NFT deposits can add vault funds to an unrelated position manager
issues.body:
#### Technical Details

[`NftFarmStrategy.depositFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L551) validates the automation settings using the supplied `position.nft` and `position.tokenId`, but it only compares the add-liquidity `tokenId` with the validated position.

There is no equivalent comparison between `increaseParams.zap.addLiquidityParams.nft` and `position.nft`. [`NftFarmVault.beforeDeposit()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftFarmVault.sol#L774) has the same incomplete check: it verifies the `tokenId`, then approves the Sickle to pull the vault's `token0` and `token1`. Consequently, an authorized keeper can validate position `(manager A, tokenId X)` but execute the add-liquidity operation against `(manager B, tokenId X)`.

[`Automation.depositFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L415) is permissioned: the caller must be a global or custom automator holding the `NFT_DUST_DEPOSIT` permission, and the Sickle must have consented to that action.

#### Impact

Informational.

#### Recommendation

Bind both components of the add-liquidity target to the validated position:

```solidity
NftAddLiquidity calldata addLiquidity =
    increaseParams.zap.addLiquidityParams;

if (
    addLiquidity.nft != position.nft
        || addLiquidity.tokenId != position.tokenId
) {
    revert DepositPositionMismatch();
}
```

Apply the same validation in [`NftFarmVault.beforeDeposit()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftFarmVault.sol#L774) as defense in depth.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894, commit 0f712546.

- `depositFor()` binds the zap's `addLiquidityParams.nft`/`tokenId` to the validated position.
- Added regression tests for the mismatch.

issues.title: A stale multi-compound target can receive rewards after ownership changes
The Arbitrum gas adapter cannot accurately price the variable L1 poster fee
Automated exits and rebalances do not bind the removal source to the authorized NFT
Some automated NFT harvest paths use the manual fee selector
Shift rebalance targets can remain immediately eligible, forcing repeatable same-range rebalances
Automation leaves economic execution choices to trusted keepers
issues.body:
Automation verifies the Sickle owner's action consent, automator authorization, and several action-specific position constraints. The opt-in is not a complete specification of every execution detail or economic outcome, so the approved automator or keeper remains a trusted role with significant responsibility over the positions that opt into automation.

#### Technical Details

The authorization layer checks whether a caller may perform an automation category for a Sickle, while downstream strategies validate the position and selected integration to varying degrees. Many arguments remain keeper-supplied because their safety or economic quality is difficult to fully express and enforce on-chain. Owners should therefore understand an automation opt-in as trust in the keeper to submit valid, conservative, and policy-compatible parameters.

Examples of keeper-controlled choices or outcomes include:

- `SwapParams` fields such as `tokenIn`, `amountIn`, `tokenApproval`, `router`, and `minAmountOut`, together with opaque aggregator `extraData` that may encode recipients and other routing choices.
- Rebalance target ticks and price context. Exact tick checks can confirm the submitted range matches a pre-operation spot-tick calculation, but they do not by themselves prove that the range remains economically appropriate after keeper-controlled swaps or market movement.
- Desired amounts, minimum amounts, swap routes, and other slippage or price-impact parameters. A call may satisfy structural pool and position checks while providing little value, obtaining poor execution, or leaving the position immediately eligible for another operation.
- Keeper-selected fee-token and sweep-token arrays, which can omit expected fee assets or include unrelated balances where the downstream path does not derive the lists from actual results.
- Opaque integration-specific claim, deposit, withdrawal, and callback data, plus generic `executeFor` registrations that may select a route without typed vault callbacks or their associated safeguards.

These examples are not additional claims that every path is exploitable. They illustrate the boundary between invariants that can be checked on-chain and execution quality, route safety, and integration behavior that still require trusted keeper operation, careful off-chain validation, and monitoring.

#### Impact

Informational.

#### Recommendation

Document the keeper trust assumptions for every automation category and require keepers to simulate the exact calldata, validate recipients and spend limits, use conservative minimums, and check the post-operation state before submitting transactions.

#### Developer Response

Documented in [vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/894), commit d4701c3b.

- `docs/AutomationKeeperTrust.md` states the enforced/trusted boundary and lists which config fields are advisory keeper inputs rather than on-chain constraints.

issues.title: Wildcard permissions silently expand when future actions are introduced
issues.body:
[`AutomationPermissions.ALL`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/libraries/AutomationPermissions.sol#L36) is defined as `type(uint256).max`, so it includes permission bits that are not yet assigned. An automator or Sickle owner using this wildcard can therefore gain or grant access to future automation categories without a new review or explicit consent transaction.

#### Technical Details

`ALL` was changed from a bitmap of defined permissions to `type(uint256).max`. `Automation.setApprovedAutomator()` assigns this value by default.

An automator granted `ALL` therefore automatically receives every permission bit introduced in the future, without a new administrative review or grant. Owners who use the same wildcard for `actionConsent` likewise pre-consent to future action categories whose risk and behavior did not exist when consent was given.

The separate owner-consent check reduces current exposure when owners consent only to explicit bits, but it does not protect wildcard consent.

#### Impact

Informational.

#### Recommendation

Define `ALL` as the union of currently supported permission bits, such as `(1 << 17) - 1`, and require explicit updates when new categories are introduced. Avoid exposing an unbounded wildcard as the default for automator permissions or owner action consent.

#### Developer Response

Acknowledged, no change. Wildcard permissions are ours, not users'. Introducing a new action bit is a deliberate deployment step, not something that happens implicitly.

issues.title: Automation unnecessarily exposes its internal batching helper
issues.body:
`Automation` inherits the external [`multicall()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/base/NonDelegateMulticall.sol#L42) entrypoint even though its batching functionality is intended only for self-calls from the automation entrypoints. This unnecessarily expands the contract's external surface, couples automation to the Sickle caller whitelist, and adds avoidable execution overhead.

#### Technical Details

The batched variants of `compoundFor()`, `harvestFor()`, `exitFor()`, and `rebalanceFor()` build arrays of targets and calldata before invoking `this.multicall(targets, data)`. Because `multicall()` is inherited from `NonDelegateMulticall`, it remains externally callable and authorizes callers through `SickleRegistry.isWhitelistedCaller()`.

No external caller is expected to use `Automation.multicall()`, yet every caller allowed by the registry-wide Sickle security model can reach it. This creates an unnecessary permissioned entrypoint whose behavior and safety depend on the Sickle caller and target whitelists. It also requires the `Automation` contract itself to remain configured as a whitelisted caller so that its self-calls succeed. Registry changes can therefore unexpectedly break automation or broaden access to a batching surface that automation does not need to expose.

The external self-call also incurs ABI encoding, calldata copying, and an unnecessary caller-whitelist lookup compared with an internal batching helper.

#### Impact

Informational.

#### Recommendation

Move the batching loop into an internal helper and call it directly from the automation entrypoints. If preserving the external self-call is required, restrict `multicall()` in `Automation` to `msg.sender == address(this)` instead of relying on `isWhitelistedCaller()`.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#895, landed on `main` via #891, commit b21233d3.

- `multicall()` is disabled externally with `MulticallDisabled`; batching moved to an internal `_multicall()`.

issues.title: Automated rebalances can remove liquidity from an unauthorized NFT
issues.body:
[`rebalanceFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L670) validates automation settings for one NFT but allows the keeper to select a different NFT as the liquidity-removal source. An authorized automator can therefore alter or burn a Sickle-owned position for which automatic rebalancing was not enabled.

#### Technical Details

`NftFarmStrategy.rebalanceFor()` constructs the validated `NftKey` from `params.position.nft` and `params.position.tokenId`. The preflight helper `ShiftMath._checkRebalanceTargetBindingsInner()` validates the replacement's `addLiquidityParams`, including its manager and fresh-mint token ID, but does not validate `params.withdraw.zap.removeLiquidityParams` against the same key. `_rebalance()` then passes this independent withdrawal structure to `_withdraw()`. `NftZapLib.zapOut()` selects a connector from `removeLiquidityParams.nft` and calls `removeLiquidity()` with the independently supplied `removeLiquidityParams.tokenId`.

Neither field is required to match the NFT manager and token ID in the validated key. A keeper can make validation succeed with an out-of-range position A, remove liquidity from another Sickle-owned position B, and use the proceeds to mint position C in A's configured pool. The post-mint checks only validate C's pool identity and ticks, so the transaction can succeed while B is altered or burned and A's settings are migrated to C.

#### Impact

Low. An authorized automator can bypass per-position rebalance consent and partially or fully remove liquidity from another Sickle-owned NFT.

#### Recommendation

Extend `ShiftMath._checkRebalanceTargetBindingsInner()` with the removal-source binding next to the existing add-liquidity target checks. Require `params.withdraw.zap.removeLiquidityParams.nft` to equal `key.nftManager` and its `tokenId` to equal `key.tokenId` before `_rebalance()` executes.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894, commit 0f712546. Same binding as #4.

issues.title: Compound targets remain usable after an NFT leaves Sickle custody
issues.body:
[`compoundFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L614) validates persisted settings and the target NFT identity, but it does not verify that the NFT is still owned by the Sickle or remains staked on its behalf. If the NFT leaves Sickle custody while its settings remain enabled, an approved automator can direct Sickle-held rewards or idle balances into the stale position.

#### Technical Details

`NftSettingsRegistry.validateCompoundFor()` checks only the `automateRewards` flag and compound behavior stored under the `(sickle, nftManager, tokenId)` key. `ShiftMath.checkCompoundTargetBindings()` additionally requires `addLiquidityParams.nft` and `addLiquidityParams.tokenId` to match the supplied position. These checks establish calldata identity, but do not query `ownerOf()` or connector-specific staking state to establish current custody.

`simpleWithdraw()` and `simpleExit()` transfer the NFT out through `_transferOutNft()` without clearing its settings. An approved keeper can subsequently call `compoundFor()` with `inPlace = true`, which skips the farm withdrawal and redeposit steps and invokes `_zapIn()` directly. The zap consumes balances held by the Sickle and the selected connector increases liquidity on the persisted manager and token ID. For connectors that permit or otherwise authorize this increase, the funds are added to an NFT controlled by its new owner.

#### Impact

Low. An approved automator can cause Sickle-owned rewards or idle assets to be irreversibly added to an NFT that is no longer controlled by the Sickle. The issue is limited to configured compound targets and does not directly transfer the NFT principal.

#### Recommendation

- Clear automation settings when an NFT leaves Sickle custody, or
- Require current Sickle ownership or recognized Sickle staking before
  compounding.

The check should validate custody immediately before the add-liquidity action,
not merely when settings are first stored.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894, commit 2c9f02dd.

- Custody check in `ShiftMath.checkCompoundTargetBindings()`, which `compoundFor()` already calls, so it costs the strategy two extra arguments.
- Follow-up in #899 (202af112) and #901 (fea13fda, 191e88c4) — see #2 for the connector-level detail.
- We chose this over clearing settings on transfer-out: the registry's unset does not cascade to settings modules, so clearing would have left the MultiCompound equivalent untouched and needed a new Sickle-callable unset on a contract deployed to 51 chains.

issues.title: Batched gas-account reimbursements duplicate transaction-wide fixed fees
issues.body:
[`Automation.executeFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L710) charges each item in a batch independently, but some gas-cost adapters include components that are incurred only once by the outer transaction. On affected chains, a keeper can therefore receive repeated reimbursement for one fixed cost and progressively deplete opted-in Sickles' prepaid gas balances.

#### Technical Details

`executeFor()` invokes `_executeOne()` for every batch item. After the strategy call, `_executeOne()` measures that item's strategy gas and calls `_chargeGasAccount()`, which invokes `IGasCostAdapter.txCost()` and immediately charges the resulting amount from the Sickle's `GasAccount`. The adapter receives each item separately, so the calculation has no context for fixed costs already shared by the enclosing transaction.

Some adapter components are fixed once per outer blockchain transaction:

- `OpStackGasCostAdapter._operatorFee()` adds `operatorFeeConstant` to every item;
- `EtherlinkGasCostAdapter.txCost()` adds `inclusionFixedBytes × inclusionFeePerByte` to every item.

For a batch of `N` operations, the chain charges one transaction-wide fixed component, while the keeper receives it `N` times from users' gas accounts. The code comment in `_executeOne()` explicitly states that transaction-wide fixed costs must not be charged per item, but the adapters do exactly that.

Independent calls to an L1 fee oracle with each inner payload can introduce further duplicated envelope overhead, although the explicit constants alone establish the overcharge.

#### Impact

Low. Batched automation can systematically overcharge gas-account-mode Sickles and exhaust prepaid balances faster than the keeper's actual transaction cost, particularly when many lightweight operations are included in one transaction.

#### Recommendation

Calculate transaction-wide fixed components once in `executeFor()` and allocate them across the batch, or make adapters return only genuinely marginal per-operation costs. Data-fee and envelope calculations should likewise account for the outer transaction once before distributing the resulting cost among the operations.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in [vfat-io/sickle-contracts#895](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/895), landed on `main` via #891, commit b21233d3.

- `IGasCostAdapter.txCost()` takes `batchSize` and shares the transaction-wide components across the batch.
- ABI break: selector `0x302bf43f` → `0x8a563399`. `Automation` and the adapter must be deployed together.

issues.title: Rollup fee oracles are queried with inner strategy calldata rather than the priced transaction
issues.body:
[`Automation._chargeGasAccount()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L820) passes one strategy payload to the gas-cost adapter, but the OP Stack and Scroll fee oracles price the data of the outer transaction. Gas-account-mode Sickles can therefore reimburse a keeper for a data fee that does not match the fee actually charged by the rollup.

#### Technical Details

`executeFor()` receives the strategy payload as one element of the outer `callData` array. `_executeOne()` forwards that isolated element as `data` to `_chargeGasAccount()`, which calls `IGasCostAdapter.txCost(gasUsed, data)`. The supplied bytes contain only the strategy selector and arguments. They omit the `executeFor()` selector, ABI array offsets and lengths, the other transaction arguments, and any other batch items.

[`OpStackGasCostAdapter._l1Fee()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/GasCostAdapter.sol#L106) supplies these inner bytes to `getL1Fee()`, and [`ScrollGasCostAdapter._l1Fee()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/GasCostAdapter.sol#L185) does the same. The [OP Stack documentation](https://docs.optimism.io/app-developers/guides/transactions/estimates#l1-data-fee) specifies that `getL1Fee()` takes a serialized unsigned Ethereum transaction. Likewise, the [Scroll documentation](https://docs.scroll.io/en/developers/transaction-fees-on-scroll/#l1-fee) specifies a signed, fully RLP-encoded transaction and explains that the fee depends on the transaction data's size and byte composition. The isolated strategy payload satisfies neither interface expectation.

Pricing a differently encoded inner call can either understate or overstate the keeper's actual data cost. The mismatch exists even when `executeFor()` contains only one operation and is separate from duplicating transaction-wide fees across a batch.

#### Impact

Low. Keepers can be systematically underpaid or overpaid on OP Stack and Scroll deployments. Underpayment can make otherwise valid automation uneconomic, while overpayment depletes users' capped prepaid gas balances faster than the transaction's actual cost.

#### Recommendation

Separate per-operation execution reimbursement from the transaction-wide rollup data fee. Calculate the data fee once for the complete `executeFor()` transaction and allocate that single amount across the batch using a documented deterministic rule, such as each operation's proportional contribution to the outer ABI-encoded calldata. Charge each Sickle its measured execution cost plus only its allocated share, and enforce that the aggregate data-fee allocation does not exceed the single batch-level fee.

Because the executing contract cannot reconstruct the signed RLP transaction faithfully, the approved automator can calculate the batch fee and per-Sickle allocations off-chain and submit them with the transaction. This is consistent with the automator's trusted role, while each Sickle's configured maximum charge and cadence remain on-chain limits on the submitted reimbursement. If this trust assumption is undesirable, reimburse the shared data fee once from protocol funds or restrict gas-account batches to a single Sickle.

#### Developer Response

Not fixable at this layer. Documented in [vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/894), commit d4701c3b.

issues.title: Gas-account mode can be disabled after execution but before reimbursement
issues.body:
[`Automation._executeOne()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L765) checks gas-account mode before executing a strategy, but [`Automation._chargeGasAccount()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L820) checks the mutable mode again before reimbursing the keeper. A contract-based Sickle owner can disable gas-account mode from a callback during strategy execution, causing the completed operation to skip reimbursement and cadence recording.

#### Technical Details

`_executeOne()` calls `_preflightGasAccountCadence()` before dispatching the strategy. The preflight considers a nonzero `GasAccount.maxChargeableFee` to mean gas-account mode and validates the charge cadence. `_executeOne()` then makes an untrusted external call to the selected strategy before calling `_chargeGasAccount()`.

Strategies commonly finish by sweeping assets to the Sickle owner through `TransferLib.transferTokensToUser()`. A native-token transfer gives a contract-based owner a callback. From that callback, the owner can call `GasAccount.setMaxChargeableFee(sickle, 0)`, since the setter authorizes the Sickle owner. Execution then returns to `_chargeGasAccount()`, which reads `maxChargeableFee` again and returns immediately because the cap is now zero.

The strategy's state changes persist, but the keeper receives no reimbursement and the prepaid balance is not debited. For cadence-gated permissions, `GasAccount.charge()` is never reached, so `lastChargedAt` is not updated either. A reentrancy guard on `Automation` would not prevent this sequence because the callback modifies `GasAccount` directly.

#### Impact

Low. A malicious contract-based owner can receive the benefit of an automation operation while making the keeper pay its gas cost. The owner can also avoid recording the charged-operation cadence, although keepers can mitigate repeated abuse through simulation and blacklisting.

#### Recommendation

Commit gas-account mode before entering the strategy and make that commitment immutable until settlement. A robust design is a two-phase GasAccount flow:

1. `beginCharge` validates cadence, snapshots the cap, and reserves sufficient balance or marks the Sickle as having an active charge.
2. Owner configuration and withdrawals cannot affect the committed operation.
3. `settleCharge` pays the measured amount, refunds any unused reservation, records cadence, and clears the lock.

At minimum, preserve the initial mode and force post-call settlement against a committed cap rather than re-reading `maxChargeableFee` and silently switching to fee mode. Rejecting cap changes while a charge is active would also close the callback window.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#895, landed on `main` via #891, commit b21233d3.

- Gas-account mode is committed before the strategy runs, so disabling the cap mid-execution cannot skip reimbursement.

issues.title: Generic `executeFor()` rebalances skip vault safeguards
issues.body:
[`Automation.executeFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L710) can dispatch `NftFarmStrategy.rebalanceFor()` without the vault callbacks used by the typed rebalance entrypoint. If this route is used for a vault after automatic rebalancing is enabled, an otherwise valid keeper operation can leave the vault referencing the retired NFT and bypass its rebalance loss limit.

#### Technical Details

`Automation.rebalanceFor()` calls `NftFarmVault.beforeRebalance()` before strategy execution and `NftFarmVault.onRebalance()` afterward. These callbacks snapshot the old position value, validate the replacement's value and custody, enforce `maxRebalanceLossBps`, and update `position.tokenId`. In contrast, `_executeOne()` validates the generic action and then calls the strategy directly with `strategy.call(data)`.

The `NftFarmStrategy.rebalanceFor()` selector is explicitly registered for generic `executeFor()` dispatch under `automationActions.NftFarmStrategy` in both the [Base canary deployment](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/script/deployments/8453-canary/plan.json#L415-L429) and the [Linea canary deployment](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/script/deployments/59144-canary/plan.json#L251-L265). Vault Sickles also consent to `NFT_REBALANCE` during construction. The vault deployment helper currently initializes automatic rebalancing as disabled, so reaching the faulty path additionally requires the vault admin to enable it and an authorized keeper to select the registered generic route.

[`NftFarmStrategy.rebalanceFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L670) can then retire the old NFT, mint and deposit its replacement, and migrate its settings while neither vault callback runs. The vault continues storing the old token ID because only [`NftFarmVault.onRebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftFarmVault.sol#L589) records the replacement. Subsequent deposits and redemptions resolve the retired position and revert, while the configured rebalance value floor was never enforced.

#### Impact

Low. The route is restricted to an authorized keeper and current vault deployment settings leave automatic rebalancing disabled. If enabled and the registered generic route is used, one valid rebalance can block normal vault deposits and redemptions and skip the vault's loss protection.

#### Recommendation

Remove `NftFarmStrategy.rebalanceFor()` from `automationActions.NftFarmStrategy` in the Base and Linea canary deployment plans and reject callback-dependent selectors in `executeFor()`. If generic dispatch must support vault rebalances, register immutable pre-call and post-call hooks with the action and execute both around the strategy call.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in [vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/894), commits ba265285 and d9f6696c.

- `rebalanceFor` dropped from generic `executeFor()` dispatch; it is reachable only through the typed entrypoint, which runs the vault checks.
- Both canaries updated on-chain: `actionPermission` for `0x4db46eab` is now 0. `harvestFor`/`exitFor`/`compoundFor` unchanged at 8/32/16.

issues.title: Rebalance can strand NFT automation revocations on obsolete token IDs
issues.body:
`setNftConfig()` and `unsetNftConfig()` silently accept obsolete token IDs. If a rebalance migrates settings first, a pending owner update succeeds on the empty old key while the live replacement retains the previous policy.

#### Technical Details

When an NFT position is rebalanced, the system mints a new token ID and migrates configuration from the old key to the new one. The multi-compound registry stores per-position settings in `nftConfigMap` using a key derived from `(sickle, nftManager, tokenId)`. During a rebalance, [`NftSettingsRegistry.transferNftSettings()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftSettingsRegistry.sol#L295-L331) calls [`MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.onRebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.sol#L134-L148), which copies the configuration from the old key to the new key and deletes the old entry.

An owner can call [`unsetNftConfig()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.sol#L88-L94) or [`setNftConfig()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.sol#L76-L84) to revoke or update a position's automation policy. These functions operate on the key provided by the caller without checking whether that key still represents the live position. If a keeper-triggered rebalance executes before the owner's transaction, the configuration migrates to the new token ID while the old key becomes empty. When the owner's transaction then executes, `unsetNftConfig()` deletes the already-empty old slot and emits `NftConfigUnset(oldKey)`, while `setNftConfig()` writes the updated policy only to the obsolete key. The live position at the new key retains the original policy.

The same behavior affects the core NFT settings managed by `NftSettingsRegistry`, as its own unset operation similarly does not verify the key's current status. When automation selectors are registered for generic execution through [`Automation.executeFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L710-L786), a keeper can batch the rebalance and a subsequent multi-compound operation that consumes the migrated configuration in a single transaction, using the predictable new token ID. The validation in [`MultiFarmStrategy._validateMultiCompoundFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L317-L359) and [`_checkDepositTarget()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L404-L438) reads the configuration at the new key and accepts it, allowing the operation to proceed before the owner's revocation transaction can execute.

#### Impact

Informational.

#### Recommendation

Address owner policy by a stable logical position identifier rather than by the rebalance-unstable token ID. One approach is to assign each position a monotonically increasing settings ID and map the changing `NftKey` to that ID, with rebalances updating only the key-to-ID mapping while owners mutate the configuration by stable ID. Alternatively, store a revocation epoch per `(sickle, nftManager)` or per logical position, include that epoch in the configuration, and require both migration and automated execution to match the current epoch; owner revocation then increments the epoch, invalidating both the old and migrated entries regardless of transaction ordering.

As a minimum defense, require `setNftConfig()` and `unsetNftConfig()` to accept an expected current key or version and revert when the supplied key does not match or is already empty, so stale transactions fail visibly and can be retried against the replacement key. A robust solution must also check a stable revocation nonce during every automated action to prevent a keeper from consuming the migrated policy after the owner has incremented the epoch, even when rebalance and consumption are batched in a single transaction.

#### Developer Response

Partially fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894, commit d3727657.

- Revoking a stale or absent opt-in is now rejected rather than silently succeeding.
- The general case — a revocation targeting a token ID a rebalance has since replaced — is unchanged.

issues.title: Equalizer NFPG registry accepts non-canonical targets with copied metadata
issues.body:
`EqualizerNfpgGaugeRegistry` identifies an NFPG from values reported by the candidate contract itself. A noncanonical target can copy the metadata of a genuine NFPG and be assigned `EqualizerNfpgConnector`, even though no canonical factory or voter relationship authenticates the target address.

#### Technical Details

[`EqualizerNfpgGaugeRegistry.connectorOf()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/equalizer/EqualizerNfpgGaugeRegistry.sol#L28-L65) probes the supplied `target` for `pool()`, `token0()`, `token1()`, `tickSpacing()`, and `gauge()`. It then verifies that the reported pool tuple resolves through the Thick factory and that the reported gauge is recognized by the voter. Both checks validate objects named by the target, but neither proves that `target` is the canonical NFPG associated with them. Any contract can therefore return values copied from a genuine NFPG and receive the Equalizer connector.

This classification has a custody-sensitive consequence. For a non-in-place compound, [`NftFarmStrategy.compoundFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L614-L637) reaches [`_compound()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L783-L812), which calls [`_withdrawNft()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L975-L995), performs the zap, and then calls [`_depositNft()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L953-L973). Through the classified connector, [`EqualizerNfpgConnector.withdrawNft()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/equalizer/EqualizerNfpgConnector.sol#L24-L29) calls `target.withdraw(tokenId)`, while [`depositExistingNft()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/equalizer/EqualizerNfpgConnector.sol#L12-L22) transfers the NFT directly from the Sickle to `target`. A metadata-compatible contract can make `withdraw()` a no-op, implement `IERC721Receiver`, and receive the NFT during the deposit step. No postcondition confirms that the final target is canonical or that the expected staked ownership relationship was established.

The automated [`Automation.compoundFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L493-L531) entrypoint nevertheless requires owner consent and an authorized keeper holding `NFT_COMPOUND`. The keeper is trusted to construct the execution parameters, including the farm address, so supplying such a target is not a privilege escalation under the stated threat model. The issue is the logical mismatch between the registry's intended classification and what it actually proves: connector discovery accepts structurally compatible impostors instead of authenticating Equalizer NFPG deployments.

#### Impact

Informational.

#### Recommendation

Authenticate the target address through a canonical Equalizer relationship instead of relying on metadata returned by the target. If the factory or voter exposes the canonical NFPG for a pool or gauge, derive that address independently and require exact equality with `target`. If no authoritative reverse lookup exists, explicitly register supported NFPG addresses in `ConnectorRegistry` rather than recognizing them heuristically.

As defense in depth, bind the owner-approved farm address and pool index to the NFT automation settings and require the keeper-supplied farm to match. After a withdrawal/deposit round trip, also verify the expected custody postcondition through a canonical connector—for example, that the Sickle again owns the unstaked NFT or that the authenticated NFPG reports the Sickle as the staked owner. These checks reduce the blast radius of routing mistakes without changing the trusted-keeper model.

#### Developer Response

Documented in [vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/894), commit d4701c3b.

- Registry contents are admin-controlled. Recorded in `docs/AutomationKeeperTrust.md` as a trusted input.

issues.title: Automated compound can override the configured unstaked custody mode
Partial rebalance can orphan the original NFT after settings migration
issues.body:
`rebalanceFor()` does not require full removal of the old position before migrating settings. A keeper can leave most liquidity on the original NFT while all policies move to a small replacement.

#### Technical Details

[`NftFarmStrategy.rebalanceFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L670-L703) accepts a keeper-supplied `NftRebalance` struct that includes a `withdraw.zap.removeLiquidityParams` field specifying the manager, token ID, and liquidity amount to remove from the old position. The function reaches [`_rebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L841-L885), which calls [`_withdraw()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L721-L730). That helper forwards these parameters directly to [`NftZapLib.zapOut()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/libraries/NftZapLib.sol#L107-L131) and then to the liquidity connector's `removeLiquidity()` method.

The in-scope [`UniswapV3Connector.removeLiquidity()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/uniswap/UniswapV3Connector.sol#L47-L78), [`UniswapV4Connector.removeLiquidity()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/uniswap/UniswapV4Connector.sol#L160-L183), and [`PancakeInfinityConnector.removeLiquidity()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/pancake/PancakeInfinityConnector.sol#L164-L187) functions implement partial liquidity removal: when the requested `liquidity` is less than the position's current liquidity, they decrease the position but do not burn the NFT. For example, `UniswapV3Connector.removeLiquidity()` burns the NFT only when the remaining liquidity reaches zero after the decrease operation.

After `_withdraw()` completes, `_rebalance()` calls [`_resetNftSettings()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L1109-L1122), which invokes [`NftSettingsRegistry.transferNftSettings()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftSettingsRegistry.sol#L295-L331). That function queries the connector for the latest token ID owned by the Sickle, assumes it represents a new replacement, and unconditionally deletes all core settings for the old `tokenId` while installing them on the new token. It then iterates over each registered settings module, such as [`MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.onRebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.sol#L134-L148), and migrates every module policy from the old key to the new key.

The pre-mint checks in [`ShiftMath.preMintRebalanceChecks()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/libraries/ShiftMath.sol#L210-L230) and the post-mint checks in [`postMintRebalanceChecks()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/libraries/ShiftMath.sol#L235-L253) verify that the replacement NFT is minted to the correct pool and, in Shift mode, to the formula-determined tick range. Neither check validates that the old NFT was burned, that all of its liquidity was removed, or that the keeper-supplied `removeLiquidityParams.nft` and `tokenId` match the configured position key. As a result, a keeper can specify a negligible removal amount, leave the old NFT live and liquid in the Sickle, and commit a state transition in which all automation policies follow a smaller replacement while the economically dominant old NFT becomes unstaked and policy-less.

#### Impact

Low. A malicious or compromised keeper can use a partial liquidity removal to leave most of the user's position in the original, still-live NFT while migrating all core settings and module policies to a newly minted replacement with minimal liquidity. The old NFT is withdrawn from its farm, loses its auto-exit, reward, rebalance, multi-compound, and stake configurations, and no longer receives farm rewards or automated risk management. The user's assets remain under Sickle custody, but normal automation follows only the small replacement.

A regular Sickle owner may manually recover or reconfigure the old NFT, though the standard position metadata still references the farm from which the malicious rebalance already withdrew it. For vault-backed Sickles with a sensibly strict `maxRebalanceLossBps`, the vault callback should revert when the orphaned value is excluded from replacement accounting, mitigating the issue in that deployment path. Vaults configured with a 100% rebalance-loss tolerance can commit the state transition and lose visibility of the orphaned NFT. The primary harm is lost farming, automation continuity, and recovery burden rather than theft.

#### Recommendation

In `rebalanceFor()`, require that `params.withdraw.zap.removeLiquidityParams.nft` equals `params.position.nft` and `params.withdraw.zap.removeLiquidityParams.tokenId` equals `params.position.tokenId` before calling `_withdraw()`. Require `params.withdraw.zap.removeLiquidityParams.liquidity` to be set to the full-removal sentinel `type(uint128).max`. After `zapOut()` completes, verify through the connector that the old token no longer exists or that its remaining liquidity is exactly zero before minting the replacement or calling `_resetNftSettings()`. Pass the strategy-discovered replacement token ID explicitly into the registry migration function and have the registry reject any populated destination key, rather than independently assuming that `getTokenId()` represents a collision-free one-for-one transition. Extend post-mint checks to assert that the old position is closed, the new position is owned by or validly staked for the same Sickle, and the new pool and range are correct.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894, commit 6f23682a.

- Automated rebalance must fully drain the source position; a partial removal reverts with `RebalancePartialRemoval`.
- We compare against live liquidity rather than restoring `nftSupplyUnchanged`: V4 and Pancake Infinity implement `totalSupply()` as `nextTokenId() - 1`, a mint counter that never decrements, so a supply check would revert every V4 rebalance while passing on V3.

issues.title: NFT claim farm is not bound to the owner's automation opt-in
issues.body:
NFT multi-compound opt-ins bind the NFT key and destination but not the source farm. A keeper can pair an enabled key with a different connector-backed source and trigger reward handling that the owner did not authorize.

#### Technical Details

The multi-compound automation feature allows Sickle owners to opt individual ERC-20 or NFT positions into keeper-driven reward consolidation. Owners configure each NFT source through [`MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.setNftConfig()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.sol#L76-L84) with a key of `(Sickle, nftManager, tokenId)` pinned to a destination farm. An authorized keeper can then trigger [`MultiFarmStrategy.nftCompoundMultipleFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L218-L235) through [`Automation.executeFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L710-L786), which should only harvest from the opted-in sources.

The validation logic in [`_validateMultiCompoundFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L317-L359) retrieves the stored NFT config using only the keeper-supplied `nftManager` and `tokenId` values, then confirms that the stored config's destination farm matches the requested one. However, this validation never binds the config to the source farm. When [`_harvestNftPositions()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L487-L518) executes, it resolves the connector from `claim.position.farm.stakingContract` and forwards `claim.harvest.extraData` directly to that connector. Neither the farm address nor the metadata contents appear in the NFT key consumed through [`MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.getNftConfig()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.sol#L118-L122).

[`LineaVestingConnector.claim()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/linea/LineaVestingConnector.sol#L59-L90) uses `position.farm.stakingContract` as the primary vesting contract address and accepts an optional `secondVestingContract` from the decoded `extraData`. When `hasGauge` is false, the connector calls `releasable(address(this))` and `release()` on both vesting contracts without referencing the validated `nftManager` or `tokenId`. An attacker-controlled keeper can therefore pair an enabled NFT key with either registered Linea vesting address, set `hasGauge = false`, and cause that vesting contract to release all tokens owed to the Sickle, bypassing the owner's per-source opt-in.

The structural mismatch means that enabling NFT key A authorizes the keeper to supply NFT key A's identity alongside source farm B's address and claim rewards from B. After the connector releases B's rewards into the Sickle via delegatecall, the same atomic transaction charges the 180-basis-point compound-for fee and executes keeper-selected swaps before depositing into the owner-pinned destination. The operation succeeds because validation never compared the supplied farm to the stored config, and malformed metadata merely causes an atomic revert.

#### Impact

Low. An authorized keeper with multi-compound permission can release all currently vested rewards from an unconfigured Linea vesting contract by pairing it with an enabled NFT key's identity. The released tokens flow through the compound-for fee calculation and keeper-selected swap routes before reaching the owner-pinned destination farm. A large vesting entitlement can suffer meaningful loss through the fixed fee and slippage, and the owner may face unwanted exposure to the destination farm's lockup or market conditions. The keeper cannot redirect the final deposit to an arbitrary address through this mechanism, but the bypass of source consent allows unauthorized handling and reallocation of rewards the owner did not opt into multi-compounding.

#### Recommendation

Add a `Farm` field to the stored `MultiCompoundConfig` in `MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry` and require the owner to record the source farm alongside the destination when calling `setNftConfig()`. Modify `_validateMultiCompoundFor()` to compare the keeper-supplied `claim.position.farm` against the stored source farm before resolving any connector. For the Linea integration, remove `secondVestingContract` from individual claim metadata and require each vesting contract to have its own enabled NFT config pinned to the same destination, or extend the config to store and validate an allowed secondary contract address. Alternatively, introduce a connector validation hook that returns a canonical list of all source contracts affected by the claim metadata and require each returned source to have an enabled config before executing any Sickle delegatecall.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894, commits 7c517ee8 and 11a20555.

- NFT sources bind to the farm recorded in their opt-in; a mismatch reverts with `SourceFarmMismatch`.
- Self-target configs must declare the source farm, enforced at write time.

Additional Linea hardening was completed in https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/917, commits 7767bc44, bdf5fa0a, and cb26a02f (merge 28df5d08).

Both vesting contracts are constructor-pinned, the payload no longer supplies a vesting address, and any optional counterpart is derived from those immutables. claim() and earned() reject unpinned primary contracts. Connector redeployment is still required for this hardening to become live.

issues.title: No-op deposits leave the ERC-20 compound target unbound from the zap pool
issues.body:
ERC-20 multi-compound settings pin only a `Farm`; the keeper independently controls the zap pool and LP token. With no-op deposit connectors, the action can create a different LP or no LP while reporting the configured target.

#### Technical Details

The multi-compound feature allows a Sickle owner to opt source positions into automated reward consolidation and pin a target farm into which those rewards should be deposited through [`MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.setErc20Config()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.sol#L98-L106). For ERC-20 targets, `MultiCompoundConfig.target` stores only the `stakingContract` and `poolIndex` fields of a `Farm` struct. When a keeper invokes [`MultiFarmStrategy.compoundMultipleFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L129-L144), the strategy validates that each source position's stored target matches `params.depositFarm` by comparing those two fields in [`_checkSourceConfig()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L378-L395). However, the actual destination asset is created earlier by [`ZapLib.zapIn()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/libraries/ZapLib.sol#L26-L96), which accepts independent keeper-supplied parameters in `params.zap.addLiquidityParams`. This structure includes the liquidity router, pool-specific data, and the resulting LP token address, none of which are validated against the owner-pinned target configuration.

After harvesting rewards and charging fees, [`_compoundMultiple()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L146-L187) invokes `ZapLib.zapIn()` with the keeper's zap parameters, then resolves the connector for `params.depositFarm.stakingContract` and calls `deposit(params.depositFarm, params.zap.addLiquidityParams.lpToken, ...)`. The [`CurvePoolConnector.deposit()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/curve/CurvePoolConnector.sol#L105-L111), [`MerklConnector.deposit()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/MerklConnector.sol#L96-L103), and [`HydrexMerklConnector.deposit()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/HydrexMerklConnector.sol#L100-L106) implementations are no-ops because the LP token remains in the Sickle, so they ignore both the `Farm` argument and the token parameter and return successfully without verifying any relationship between the pinned farm and the supplied LP token.

`ZapLib.zapIn()` treats `addLiquidityParams.lpToken == address(0)` as an early successful return after executing swaps, skipping the `addLiquidity` step entirely. A no-op connector's `deposit()` then succeeds without performing any destination operation. In both variants, the final transaction emits events referencing the stored farm, while the actual pool used by the zap may differ or no liquidity may have been added at all.

#### Impact

Low. A keeper holding the MULTI_COMPOUND permission can convert a user's newly claimed rewards into an LP position from a different supported pool than the owner-pinned target, or complete the operation without adding liquidity by supplying a zero LP token. The resulting assets remain owned by the Sickle and the source principal is not withdrawn, so the operation does not steal funds. The owner can sweep or unwind the assets using standard Sickle controls. The residual harm includes unauthorized market exposure, recovery costs to unwind unwanted positions, misleading compound events that report the pinned farm rather than the actual pool, protocol fees charged despite no target deposit when the zero-LP variant is used, and the potential for one reimbursed ineffective operation per gas-account cadence.

#### Recommendation

Reject `lpToken == address(0)` in `compoundMultipleFor()` before harvesting to prevent no-deposit variants. Extend `MultiCompoundConfig` for ERC-20 targets to include the canonical destination LP token address and, where applicable, the liquidity router or pool identifier. Before invoking `ZapLib.zapIn()`, validate that `params.zap.addLiquidityParams.lpToken` and related pool fields match the stored target configuration. For connectors that implement no-op deposits, add explicit target validation rather than relying on their `deposit()` call to enforce the relationship between the pinned farm and the supplied token. Emit the validated LP token or pool identifier in compound events so monitoring systems reflect the actual destination used.

#### Developer Response

Partially fixed in vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894, commit 8d96cf82.

- A zero destination `lpToken` is rejected before harvesting, rather than charging the fee, running the swaps and depositing nothing.
- The general case stays open: the no-op deposit connectors (Curve pool, Merkl, HydrexMerkl) ignore both farm and token by design, because the LP stays in the Sickle.

issues.title: Pangolin rewards are irrecoverably routed to strategy contracts
Owner-configured rebalance loss limits are not enforced
issues.body:
`NftSettingsRegistry` stores owner-selected slippage, price-impact, and dust limits for automated rebalances, but `rebalanceFor()` never consumes them. These settings therefore do not constrain the keeper-supplied swap and liquidity parameters used during execution.

#### Technical Details

The owner-facing [`RebalanceConfig`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/structs/NftSettingsStructs.sol#L27-L62) contains `slippageBP`, `priceImpactBP`, and `dustBP`. When the owner enables automated rebalancing, [`NftSettingsRegistry._checkRebalanceConfig()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftSettingsRegistry.sol#L400-L443) only checks that these values fall within protocol-wide ranges before storing them. This proves that the configuration is syntactically valid, but it does not apply the selected limits to a rebalance.

At execution time, [`NftSettingsRegistry.validateRebalanceFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftSettingsRegistry.sol#L160-L196) verifies that automated rebalancing is enabled, that the current tick has crossed the configured trigger, and that it remains within the cutoff range. It does not use `slippageBP`, `priceImpactBP`, or `dustBP`. [`ShiftMath.preMintRebalanceChecks()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/libraries/ShiftMath.sol#L206-L230) loads the settings, but uses them only to bind the destination manager and pool and, when Shift mode is enabled, to derive the expected tick range. The corresponding [`postMintRebalanceChecks()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/libraries/ShiftMath.sol#L232-L253) verifies the replacement pool and ticks without checking the value retained in the new position.

After those preliminary checks, [`NftFarmStrategy.rebalanceFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L664-L703) forwards keeper-supplied parameters to [`_rebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L838-L885). The resulting zap accepts keeper-selected swap routes, `minAmountOut` values, mint minimums, and opaque router calldata. In particular, [`AggregatorConnector.swapExactTokensForTokens()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/AggregatorConnector.sol#L30-L71) only compares the amount returned to the Sickle against the `minAmountOut` supplied in the same keeper calldata. A zero minimum therefore does not enforce the owner's stored percentage limits, and the opaque router call may specify a different output recipient. A replacement NFT can still pass the pool and tick checks while containing substantially less value than the original position.

An authorized keeper is trusted under the stated threat model to construct conservative, policy-compatible execution parameters. Deliberately choosing a hostile recipient or ineffective minimum is therefore not a privilege escalation by itself. The logical issue is that the protocol exposes these three fields as owner-selected rebalance allowances, validates and migrates them with the position, but never makes them an on-chain execution constraint. Their effective enforcement depends entirely on off-chain keeper behavior.

#### Impact

Informational.

#### Recommendation

Enforce the existing owner-configured `slippageBP`, `priceImpactBP`, and `dustBP` limits stored in `NftSettingsRegistry` during automated rebalances. Derive swap and liquidity minimums from these values using a manipulation-resistant quote, require every swap output recipient to be the executing Sickle, and reject rebalances whose resulting value loss or residual dust exceeds the configured bounds.

Do not rely on keeper-supplied `minAmountOut`, desired amounts, or opaque recipient calldata as proof that the owner-selected policy was respected. If reliable on-chain enforcement is not available and these fields are intended to remain advisory, remove them from the owner-facing configuration or clearly document that they do not constrain execution.

#### Developer Response

Documented in [vfat-io/sickle-contracts#894](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/894), commit d4701c3b.

- Loss limits are advisory keeper inputs, not on-chain constraints. `docs/AutomationKeeperTrust.md` says so explicitly.

issues.title: V3 multi-compound source configurations do not bind the destination pool
Action registrations do not enforce their single-permission-bit invariant
User-controlled callbacks can attack other operations in shared automation batches
issues.body:
[`Automation.setNftRebalanceCallback()` and `Automation.setNftDepositCallback()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L208-L223) allow each Sickle owner to register arbitrary callback code. Because Automation executes these callbacks inside keeper batches without isolating different owners, a malicious callback can manipulate shared markets and vault state around unrelated users' operations, extract funds from vault shareholders, or make the complete batch revert after consuming keeper gas.

#### Technical Details

The callback setters only require `msg.sender` to equal `sickle.owner()`. They do not restrict callbacks to approved implementations or bind a callback to the integration operated by its Sickle. The authorization performed by Automation confirms that the outer caller is an approved automator and that each Sickle consented to the action, but it does not constrain the external actions performed by a callback.

[`Automation.rebalanceFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L581-L634) uses three global phases. It first invokes every `beforeRebalance()` callback, then executes every strategy operation through `multicall()`, and finally invokes every `onRebalance()` callback. A funded malicious callback can therefore trade against a pool or route in `beforeRebalance()`, leave the manipulated state in place while unrelated users rebalance, and reverse the trade in `onRebalance()`. This embeds an atomic sandwich inside the trusted keeper transaction, including when the transaction is submitted privately. The victims lose value through adverse swap execution or liquidity placement, while the attacker retains the value captured by the reverse trade. Keeper-supplied minimum outputs and liquidity minimums bound the attack but do not prevent extraction within the accepted tolerance.

The global phases also allow malicious callbacks to interleave with `NftFarmVault`'s security lifecycle. [`NftFarmVault.beforeRebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftFarmVault.sol#L563-L587) snapshots an absolute pre-rebalance value `V`, and [`NftFarmVault.onRebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftFarmVault.sol#L589-L624) later compares the replacement value against that snapshot. The `nonReentrant` guard covers each callback separately and is released between them. If a later attacker pre-hook calls the vault's public [`deposit()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/NftFarmVault.sol#L653-L717) with value `D` after the snapshot, a rebalance that incorporates the deposit and loses `L` is accepted whenever `V + D - L >= V * (1 - maxLoss)`. The actual permitted loss is therefore `D + maxLoss * V` instead of `maxLoss * V`. The callback can combine this stale snapshot with the rebalance sandwich, capture `L`, and redeem its fairly minted shares after the victim's post-hook. For example, with `V = 100`, a 1% loss limit, `D = 4`, and `L = 5`, the final value of 99 passes the nominal 1% floor. After redeeming, the attacker can retain approximately 4.81 units taken from the original shareholders.

Exact-liquidity rebalances permit a stronger share inflation variant. Consider a batch ordered as attacker item A, victim vault, and attacker item B, where both attacker items use the same callback contract. The victim pre-hook first snapshots `V`, then B's pre-hook makes a small proportional deposit `D` into the old NFT. If the keeper encoded the old NFT's original exact liquidity, the connector removes only that amount. [`UniswapV3Connector.removeLiquidity()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/connectors/uniswap/UniswapV3Connector.sol#L47-L77) does not burn the old NFT because the callback-added liquidity remains, while the strategy creates a replacement NFT containing approximately `V`.

A's post-hook executes before the victim post-hook and can call `deposit()` again with value `E`. Vault storage still references the old NFT, so share issuance is priced against the small residual `D` and any idle pool-token balance while the replacement NFT is omitted. The callback can consequently mint approximately `E / D` times the existing share supply. The victim post-hook then resolves the replacement NFT, verifies its value against the original snapshot, and updates the stored token ID. B's post-hook can immediately redeem the inflated shares from the replacement. With `V = 100`, `D = 0.01`, and `E = 0.99`, the attacker can obtain approximately 99% of the shares and redeem about 99 units after contributing only 1 unit. This variant requires exact-liquidity removal, an in-range and TWAP-valid residual position, suitable resolver and custody behavior, low idle balances, and deposit-cap headroom. Using `type(uint128).max` removal consumes the callback-added seed and prevents this particular transition, but leaves the stale loss-floor attack described above.

[`Automation.depositFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/221a7d22fcc7a5fe2fb5ecc9e9ffe493b2353d7c/contracts/Automation.sol#L415-L455) executes each item as `beforeDeposit()` followed by its strategy deposit. Two attacker-controlled entries can bracket victim entries because the function does not reject duplicate Sickles or isolate owners. The first callback can manipulate a shared pool, the victim deposits can then swap or add liquidity at the manipulated state, and the second callback can reverse the trade. The attacker Sickles can use negligible operations in unrelated pools because their callbacks are not restricted to the corresponding positions. Victim loss is again bounded only by the keeper's execution minimums.

Finally, either callback can deliberately revert, exhaust the remaining gas, or perform expensive external work before returning. Any revert rolls back the complete mixed-user batch, and both failed and successful expensive callbacks charge gas to the keeper. One malicious job can therefore block unrelated jobs or repeatedly impose transaction costs until the keeper identifies and excludes it. There is no callback gas limit or failure isolation.

#### Impact

Medium. A malicious Sickle owner included in a mixed keeper batch can extract value from unrelated Sickles and vault shareholders, bypass a vault's configured rebalance loss limit, and under narrower exact-liquidity conditions inflate shares and drain most of a replacement position. The attacker can also revert complete batches or impose arbitrary gas costs on the keeper. The attacks require attacker-controlled jobs to be co-batched with victims, and the strongest paths additionally depend on ordering, liquidity-removal parameters, position state, and vault cap headroom.

#### Recommendation

Restrict callback registration to approved, immutable implementations, or execute callback-enabled jobs from different owners in separate transactions. For `rebalanceFor()`, cache the callback address and execute each item's `beforeRebalance()`, strategy operation, and `onRebalance()` as one isolated lifecycle. Reject duplicate or adversarially ordered entries where isolation is not guaranteed.

Add a vault-level rebalance lock that remains active from `beforeRebalance()` until `onRebalance()` and rejects deposits and redemptions during that interval. Also require the share supply to remain unchanged, ensure the old NFT is fully consumed, and price deposits against every vault asset, including any in-flight replacement NFT. If arbitrary callbacks must remain supported, apply an explicit gas limit and isolate callback failure per job rather than allowing one callback to affect an unrelated batch. Do not silently ignore a failed vault callback because the callback enforces required safety checks.

#### Developer Response

Acknowledged, no code change for this reason. We control batch composition — an attacker cannot place themselves next to a victim, so this is not attacker-reachable in practice.

- Note that restricting who may register a callback does not address this: the callback contract can own the Sickle and register itself, so `msg.sender == callback == owner` passes every check.
- Separately, in [vfat-io/sickle-contracts#906](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/906) (9183d7b6), `rebalanceFor()` now brackets each Sickle's callbacks around its own rebalance instead of running three global phases. We did that for consistency with `depositFor()`, which already worked that way, not as a mitigation.

issues.title: Shadow multi-compound can penalize pre-existing xShadow
issues.body:
`ShadowRewardBehavior.Exit` processes the Sickle's complete xShadow balance rather than only newly claimed rewards. An authorized keeper can therefore apply the exit penalty to xShadow retained from unrelated positions or earlier operations.

#### Technical Details

The multi-compound strategy allows a Sickle owner to configure automated consolidation of specific farm positions into a pinned destination. Shadow V2 and V3 gauge connectors support three reward behaviors: `Exit` (approximately 50% penalty to liquid SHADOW), `X33` (no-penalty deposit), and `Keep` (retain as xShadow). The owner binds source and destination farms in [`MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/MultiCompoundSettingsRegistry.sol#L83-L117), and the automated [`compoundMultipleFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L151-L177) and [`nftCompoundMultipleFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L255-L285) paths require the owner to grant `MULTI_COMPOUND` permission.

When an authorized keeper calls either entry point, [`_validateMultiCompoundFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L366-L424) validates that every source was opted into automation with the supplied destination farm. The keeper also supplies claim parameters for each source, including opaque `extraData` fields. [`ShadowV2GaugeConnector.claim()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/connectors/shadow/ShadowV2GaugeConnector.sol#L38-L48) and [`ShadowV3GaugeConnector.claim()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/connectors/shadow/ShadowV3GaugeConnector.sol#L39-L60) decode this data as a `ShadowRewardBehavior` enum.

[`MultiFarmStrategy._harvestErc20Positions()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L585-L608) and [`_harvestNftPositions()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/MultiFarmStrategy.sol#L610-L640) forward the keeper-controlled `extraData` directly to the resolved connector through [`sickle.multicall()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/base/Multicall.sol#L42-L75). The Shadow connectors permit `ShadowRewardBehavior.Exit`.

After calling `getReward()`, both [`ShadowV2GaugeClaim._claimGaugeRewards()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/connectors/shadow/ShadowGaugeClaim.sol#L61-L76) and [`ShadowV3GaugeClaim._claimGaugeRewards()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/connectors/shadow/ShadowGaugeClaim.sol#L41-L57) read the Sickle's complete xShadow balance with `IERC20(X_SHADOW).balanceOf(address(this))`. When the keeper has selected `Exit`, the full balance is passed to `IXShadow.exit(rewards)`, triggering the approximately 50% penalty on the entire amount rather than only the newly claimed rewards for the opted-in source.

This behavior applies to xShadow accumulated from other positions, prior manual operations, and any prior `Keep` decisions. The owner's source-specific opt-in and the strategy's source-farm validation do not constrain which xShadow is affected. Because the connectors execute in the Sickle's context via delegatecall, `address(this)` resolves to the victim's Sickle, and the balance query captures all xShadow at rest in that account.

#### Impact

Low. A keeper can consume the Sickle's entire pre-existing xShadow balance through the penalized exit, not merely the rewards of the opted-in source. The approximately 50% penalty applies to the full amount, causing irreversible loss to the user. This affects xShadow the owner previously retained using the `Keep` behavior, including balances from unrelated positions and manual actions. The transaction completes atomically with valid destination deposits and emits successful compound events, giving no indication that a large pre-existing balance was forcibly exited at the penalized rate.

#### Recommendation

Snapshot xShadow before the first Shadow reward call and apply `Exit` or `X33` only to the positive claim delta. If full-balance conversion remains useful, expose it as a separate owner-only operation rather than claim `extraData` available to automation. Add an automated multi-compound regression test proving that the starting xShadow balance cannot decrease.

#### Developer Response

Acknowledged but doesn't need fixing as we don't use Keep in production when building calldata, and so this hasn't occurred (also being a small dex at this point).

issues.title: Manual cross-pool rebalance migrates stale automation policy
issues.body:
A manual rebalance can mint the replacement NFT in a different pool while automatically preserving the original pool's exit and rebalance settings. Subsequent automation therefore evaluates Pool A's price while operating on the replacement position in Pool B.

#### Technical Details

[`NftFarmStrategy.rebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L270-L277) is an owner-triggered path and intentionally accepts caller-supplied rebalance parameters without the keeper-only target checks used by `rebalanceFor()`. Through the nested add-liquidity parameters, the owner can mint a replacement position in another pool supported by the same NFT manager.

Allowing that manual mint is not itself the issue. The inconsistency arises because [`_rebalance()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L883-L918) calls `_resetNftSettings()` immediately after the new NFT is minted. [`NftSettingsLib.transferNftSettings()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/libraries/NftSettingsLib.sol#L18-L31) reads the original settings and forwards them unchanged to [`NftSettingsRegistry.transferNftSettings()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/NftSettingsRegistry.sol#L320-L358), which stores them under the newly minted token ID. The migrated values still contain Pool A's `pool`, `poolId`, exit triggers, and rebalance policy even when the new token belongs to Pool B.

The registry does not establish that the new token belongs to the stored pool. When `autoRebalance` is enabled, [`_checkTickWidth()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/NftSettingsRegistry.sol#L554-L574) compares the new position's width with Pool A's tick spacing, but it does not derive the new position's pool identity. A Pool B position with a compatible tick spacing and width therefore passes. When only `autoExit` is enabled, even this width check is skipped and no position-to-pool consistency check is performed.

The resulting settings entry combines a Pool B token ID with Pool A policy. [`validateExitFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/NftSettingsRegistry.sol#L258-L280) reads Pool A's tick to evaluate the migrated exit thresholds, while [`exitFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L669-L703) binds liquidity removal to the current token ID in Pool B. Pool B can consequently be exited solely because Pool A crossed the old threshold.

The rebalance path has a stronger consequence. [`rebalanceFor()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L711-L744) loads the migrated settings and passes them to the keeper-only checks. [`ShiftMath`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/libraries/ShiftMath.sol#L325-L374) evaluates Pool A's tick against Pool B's current range, requires the replacement mint to resolve to the stored Pool A identity, and accepts the final position when that condition holds. A successful automated call can therefore fully remove Pool B's liquidity and remint the proceeds into Pool A.

This requires a cross-pool manual rebalance under the same NFT manager and a farm connector that accepts the replacement position or performs no custody-changing deposit. It can arise from an integration error or from using `rebalance()` for an intentional cross-pool reposition. The separate [`move()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/strategies/NftFarmStrategy.sol#L285-L332) path already supports such moves while accepting explicit replacement settings.

#### Impact

Low. An honest keeper following the migrated on-chain policy can prematurely exit a Pool B position based on Pool A's price or move Pool B's principal back into Pool A. The user retains control of the funds, but incurs unintended swaps, protocol fees, slippage, interrupted yield, and exposure to a pool the manual transaction had replaced. The prerequisite is an owner-triggered cross-pool call through `rebalance()` rather than `move()`, which limits likelihood but does not require a malicious keeper payload.

#### Recommendation

Before migrating settings, construct the old position's `NftKey` and load its settings through `nftSettingsRegistry.getNftSettings(key)`. After `_zapIn()` mints the replacement, retrieve `newTokenId` before calling `_resetNftSettings()`. If `autoExit` or `autoRebalance` is enabled, call the existing [`shiftMath.postMintRebalanceChecks()`](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/blob/73a21e53fbeaf4a2212c96c92336772838b0e76b/contracts/libraries/ShiftMath.sol#L353-L374) with `isShift = false` and zero expected ticks. In this mode, the function executes `_verifyMintPoolIdentityInner()` but skips `_verifyShiftTicksInner()`, providing the required pool-identity check without any new helper or refactoring.

Only call `_resetNftSettings()` after this check succeeds. A pool mismatch will then revert before stale policy is transferred; the owner can instead use `move()` with explicit replacement settings. Limiting the check to positions with `autoExit` or `autoRebalance` preserves unrestricted manual rebalances for positions without pool-sensitive automation. No storage-layout or settings migration change is required.

#### Developer Response

Fixed in [PR #925](https://github.com/vfat-io/sickle-contracts/pull/925).
